frames.label: In US practice, engineering drawings generally present small dimensions in decimal inches (e.g., 0.002"), while speci...
frames.main_point: In US practice, engineering drawings generally present small dimensions in decimal inches (e.g., 0.002"), while specification documents may use either decimal inches or mils. This reflects differing conventions between drawings and specs rather than a strict universal rule.
frames.source_quote: On a drawing it would always be 0.002".  In a specification document it could be either.
frames.subject: unit notation on drawings vs specifications (mils vs decimal inches)

frames.label: There is no commonly used standalone symbol for mil/thou in US practice; the word "mils" is written out in documentation
frames.main_point: There is no commonly used standalone symbol for mil/thou in US practice; the word "mils" is written out in documentation. The spelling is "mils," not "mills."
frames.source_quote: I'm not aware of any.  We just always wrote "mils" (not "mills")
frames.subject: symbol usage for mil/thou

frames.label: In US precision machining, 0.0001 inch (one ten-thousandth) is colloquially called a "tenth" (i.e., a tenth of a thou...
frames.main_point: In US precision machining, 0.0001 inch (one ten-thousandth) is colloquially called a "tenth" (i.e., a tenth of a thousandth). This term is shop talk and not typically used in formal specifications.
frames.source_quote: Colloquially, I know that people in precision machine shops refer to 0.1 mils (0.0001") as "tenths" (as in one ten thousandth of an inch).
frames.subject: "tenths" terminology for 0.0001 inch

frames.label: In US customary practice, sub-inch dimensions are expressed as decimal inches, with optional prefixes or scientific n...
frames.main_point: In US customary practice, sub-inch dimensions are expressed as decimal inches, with optional prefixes or scientific notation for very small values. There is no separate base unit below the inch.
frames.source_quote: For US customary units, there's nothing smaller than an inch, you just start adding more zeros, applying prefixes, or using scientific notation.
frames.subject: representation of sub-inch dimensions in US customary units

frames.label: In US documentation, surface roughness is commonly specified in microinches
frames.main_point: In US documentation, surface roughness is commonly specified in microinches. This is a standard usage for expressing small-scale surface finish.
frames.source_quote: For example, it would be common to specify surface roughness in microinches.
frames.subject: surface roughness units in US practice

frames.label: A microinch equals one millionth of an inch (10^-6 in)
frames.main_point: A microinch equals one millionth of an inch (10^-6 in).
frames.source_quote: A microinch is one millionth (¹⁄₁₀₀₀₀₀₀) of an inch. Labeled as din.
frames.subject: microinch (din)

frames.label: One millimeter equals 0.0393701 inches; to convert dimensions from millimeters to inches, multiply by 0.0393701
frames.main_point: One millimeter equals 0.0393701 inches; to convert dimensions from millimeters to inches, multiply by 0.0393701.
frames.subject: millimeter to inch conversion factor
frames.thread_title: What is the suitable multiplier for all units?

frames.label: The modern inch is defined as exactly 25.4 millimeters
frames.main_point: The modern inch is defined as exactly 25.4 millimeters. Use 25.4 as the exact conversion factor between inches and millimeters with no rounding.
frames.source_quote: The new standards gave an inch of exactly 25.4 mm, 1.7 millionths of an inch longer than the old imperial inch and 2 millionths of an inch shorter than the old US inch.
frames.subject: inch-to-millimeter exact conversion
frames.thread_title: What is the suitable multiplier for all units?
